summary.text: 页 is the standardized simplified form of 頁. The traditional graph is a head-and-body pictograph; it was also used as a common spelling for 葉, the separate word for “page” or “sheet.”

formation.text: 页 is a derived form of the pictographic traditional graph 頁. That graph is analyzed as a kneeling person with the head emphasized; the analysis concerns 頁 and does not establish separate components in modern 页.

history.text: Ancient forms of 頁 are described as showing a kneeling person with the head emphasized. Some oracle-bone forms include hair and others omit it; later forms may distort the hair as 止, while the small-seal form omits it. The curated seal-style image is a modern drawing of that script form, not an ancient artifact.

Accounts differ on the traditional graph’s internal analysis: one describes 卩 with 首, while the received Shuowen wording gives 𦣻 with 几. A later textual-critical note disputes that wording. 頁 and 首 are also described as graphic variants distinguished by whether the body is drawn.

页 is identified as the standardized simplified form of 頁. A separate account links its shape to cursive 頁, but the precise graphic path is unresolved; the traditional graph’s pictorial analysis should not be assigned to modern 页 as an internal breakdown.

uncertainties.text: The reported use of 頁 as a common spelling for 葉 is a proposed borrowing for a different word, rather than a demonstrated change from “head” to “page.” Its earliest dated use and the historical sound match behind the borrowing remain unresolved.

Descriptions of ancient forms and their contexts come through database analyses; individual artifact images were not independently inspected. One isolated bronze phrase is considered possibly abbreviated or erroneous.

senses.gloss: head, including pig’s head in the cited oracle-bone contexts
senses.text: Oracle-bone contexts are interpreted as referring to a pig’s head and to bowing the head. These are documented early uses of traditional 頁; they do not identify the original spoken name of the pictured head.
Modern 页 writes the page or sheet word through traditional 頁, which was used as a common spelling for 葉. This is a borrowed spelling, not an established semantic development from “head.”
“Leaf” is listed alongside page and sheet, but its dating and whether it is an independent single-character use are unresolved.

developments.text: Traditional 頁, used for “head,” was also used as a common spelling for 葉, the separate word associated with pages or sheets. The proposed mechanism is that the words may have sounded alike or similarly; the historical sound match is not demonstrated here.

limitations.text: A verified earliest dated attestation and dated sequence for page, sheet, and leaf uses are not supplied; those glosses alone do not establish their chronology.
The recorded yè and xié readings and the reported fanqie for the head reading do not independently establish the historical sound relation behind the 葉 borrowing.

overview.text: 页 is the simplified form of 頁, a traditional picture of a kneeling person with the head emphasized. 頁 was proposed as a spelling for 葉, “page” or “sheet,” because the words may have sounded alike; that historical sound match remains unproven.

takeaway.text: The page meaning comes from borrowing the spelling for 葉; it is not a known change in the meaning of “head.”

relationships.text: 页 is identified as the standardized simplified form of 頁. Another account links its shape to cursive 頁, but the specific graphic path is unresolved.

In the head sense, 頁 and 首 are described as variants of one head pictograph, distinguished by whether the body is drawn. This is a relationship between traditional graphs, not a breakdown of modern 页.
